newsitem.title: GERMANY: Shortened German work week finds few backers.
newsitem.headline: Shortened German work week finds few backers.

text.p: A proposal by German union leader Klaus Zwickel to create jobs by cutting the length of the work week won little support on Thursday with employers, the government and press all fearing it could hurt the economy.

In a surprise suggestion, Zwickel on Wednesday said that the work week in the engineering sector should be trimmed by three hours from its current 35 and called for unions in other sectors, which still have longer working weeks, to seek a 35-hour week.
But far from creating demand for additional workers, labour market leaders said they feared the plan would hurt industry and could ultimately lead to even higher unemployment.
Federal Labour Office head Bernhard Jagoda said what was needed instead was greater labour market flexibility in order to win the battle to cut Germany's 4.5 million unemployed.
"If we reduce working times step-by-step, I have the great fear that this could be offset by rationalisation," Jagoda told Saarland radio.
Jagoda said it was important to reach agreements which would increase the running time of industrial machinery to boost productivity, while offering workers more control over their job hours.

The head of the German federal employers association, Dieter Hundt, echoed the Labour Office chief, saying the deal would amount to a "death blow" for the economy and that rather than fewer hours, longer work days were needed to get the economy moving.
Switzerland, he pointed out, has a developed economy like Germany's, but workers there rack up 20 percent longer days than in Germany.

Editorials in leading newspapers said that while Zwickel had certainly secured headlines for the summit with his proposal, he had not presented a truly workable solution to Germany's record unemployment.

"His call on individual unions to place an emphasis on further cuts in the working week to resolve labour market problems will ensure that the jobs summit, which was otherwise uneventful, will produce headlines," the Handelsblatt business daily said.
Even the more liberal Frankfurter Rundschau took a cautious tone. "The attempt is daring and courageous. But the jury is still out on who will share the burden," it said.
The president of the ZDH Federation of German Building Trades, Dieter Philipp, took a more hopeful approach to Zwickel's proposal, calling it a interesting idea worthy of disucssion.

Philipp said the proposal showed the Zwickel recognised the need to cut labour costs, but added it was unreasonable for tradesmen to accept cuts in their incomes that might come as part of a reduced work week.
Zwickel's strongest support came not surprisingly from the pro-labour opposition Social Democrats (SPD).
Parliamentary leader Rudolf Scharping told journalists the proposal was an "unusual and wide-ranging offer" that could open the door to a broad discussion about how to slash joblessness.
